newsitem.title: ZAIRE: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Capital of Kabila's Congo works normally.
newsitem.headline: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Capital of Kabila's Congo works normally.

text.p: Kinshasa, capital of Laurent Kabila's new Democratic Republic of Congo, went to work normally on Monday despite opposition predictions of a stay-home protest.
Shops and offices opened and the teeming city's main market bustled. Witnesses described traffic on the main boulevards, where students protested against Kabila on Friday and Saturday, as normal.
State radio, quoting Information Minister Raphael Ghenda, reminded civil servants that Monday was a normal working day and said failure to turn up for work would result in "serious penalties."

Aides to veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, who spearheaded internal opposition to ousted Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, said on Sunday there would be a stay-home protest but added that his party was not formally calling for this.
"It's not the party which has ordered this stay-home protest, (it's) the people themselves who have decided to stage it," one adviser, Martin Tshibangu Tshimbadi, had told Reuters.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo marched into Kinshasa on May 17 to crown a seven-month civil war with victory. They initially took up arms in a dispute over denial of Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis.

Opposition activists, frustrated at Kabila's refusal to name Tshisekedi prime minister last week, denounce the presence of Rwandan, Ugandan, Burundian, Angolan and other foreign troops among Kabila's forces.
Kabila aides, who accuse Tshisekedi and his supporters of "xenophobia and racial hatred", say that he plans to name new ministers to increase the size of his government from 13 to 20.
Tshisekedi aides said they would stage new protest marches in the streets of the capital on Wednesday and Friday.
Ghenda told Reuters on Sunday that even if there was initial backing for such protests it was unlikely to last as the people wanted life to return to normal.

Ghenda said people calling stay-home protests were impatient. "They should give us the time to manage the situation in a responsible manner," he added. "Those behind this kind of action are motivated by their selfish interest."

Monday's newspapers highlighted a polarisation of views between the two sides but Le Palmares, which is close to Tshisekedi, said that Kabila had offered the veteran opposition leader the post of vice-president.
